14268340.title: File:All Saints Church, Margaret Street, W1 - entrance to the chancel - geograph.org.uk - 1529059.jpg

ObjectName.value: All Saints Church, Margaret Street, W1 - entrance to the chancel - geograph.org.uk - 1529059

Categories.value: Taken with Canon PowerShot G7|Interior of All Saints, Margaret Street|Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland|Information field template with formatting|Images by Mike Quinn|Victorian tiles|United Kingdom photographs taken on 2009-08-07|Aesthetic Movement|Floor tiles in England|Mosaics in the City of Westminster|Mosaic floors in London

ImageDescription.value: All Saints Church, Margaret Street, W1 - entrance to the chancel. See 1528965. The chancel is entered through Butterfield-designed gilt iron and brass gates (made by Potter of south Molton Street) set into a low screen of alabaster and marble - see http://www.allsaintsmargaretstreet.org.uk/history5.htm. Butterfield's tiled floor, made by Minton, is deep red with black checks and a white stone diaper, while the north and south aisles have a triangular variation on this pattern - see http://www.allsaintsmargaretstreet.org.uk/history2.htm.

ObjectName.value: Spring Hall Halifax 017

Categories.value: Taken with Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ9|Interior of Spring Hall, Halifax|Self-published work|Victorian tiles

ImageDescription.value:
Interior of Spring Hall, now known as Spring Hall Mansions, off Huddersfield Road, Halifax, West Yorkshire. Showing a surprisingly plain fire-surround in the first-floor chamber which would have been an important front bedroom. However the surround may be figured marble beneath the paint - or possibly wood which was hand-painted with Arts and Crafts symbols such as natural flowers. The ironwork is hand-crafted. The tiles are Victorian, and if they are original, then they would be hand-made.

This mansion was a rebuild of a 17th century house, and designed in 1871 by William Swinden Barber for Tom Holdsworth. It is owned by Kirklees Council and it houses Calderdale Register Office.

Note: Most of the interior of the building is not accessible to the public. Each interior image by this uploader was taken with kind permission of Council staff.

13629557.title: File:St Andrew's church - rood screen detail - geograph.org.uk - 933416.jpg

ObjectName.value: St Andrew's church - rood screen detail - geograph.org.uk - 933416

Categories.value: Taken with Canon PowerShot S3 IS|Floor tiles|Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland|Saint Walstan|Information field template with formatting|Images by Evelyn Simak|Victorian tiles|St Andrew, Great Ryburgh (interior)

ImageDescription.value: St Andrew's church - rood screen detail Two panels of the C20 rood screen, depicting St Walstan (at left) and St Felix. St Andrew's church > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933385 - https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933392 has a round tower of Saxon workmanship > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933375 - the octagonal bellstage is a 14th century addition - and a south and north transept dating from the 14th century also. The church and surrounding churchyard are hemmed in by a wall and tall trees from all sides and hence difficult to photograph. Extensively restored in Victorian times, the probably most notable feature of St Andrew's is the stained glass > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933423 - https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933421 by William Wailes, dating from the mid-19th century. The chancel is the work of Sir Ninian Comper, who also designed the alabaster reredos > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933397 - https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933402. Remains of an old stone tomb > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933409 can be seen on the chancel north wall; it is believed to have been constructed from parts of several different tombs, with the lower part having come from the tomb of Thomas Buttes, d. 1592. The ledger slab seen on the floor in front is to members of the Bacon family. The C20 rood screen below the south transept arch > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933412 - its panels are painted with a sequence of saints (two panels seen here) - was erected in the memory of the fallen in WWI. The font > https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/933431 is Victorian and its cover dates from the 20th century but the surrounding floor tiles are C14. See also: http://www.norfolkchurches.co.uk/greatryburgh/greatryburgh.htm

ImageDescription.value: St Michael's church - Victorian floor tiles. St Michael's church is hemmed in by houses from all sides > 1300902 and difficult to reach. Although its tower can occasionally be glimpsed over roofs and through trees, there is only a narrow driveway > 1300904 and a short section of path leading to it. The churchyard contains a number of interesting old headstones and the remains of an ancient stone cross > 1300916 are situated right in front of the south porch which dates from the 15th century. The main body of the church > 1300908 was built a century earlier and the chancel wall contains lumps of carstone. The church interior > 1300927 was extensively restored by the architect G.E. Pritchett in the mid-19th century. It was during this time that the stained glass was put in many of the windows. According to the Norfolk churches website, St Michael's contains probably the best collection of late 19th and early 20th century glass of any small church in East Anglia > 1300958 - 1300968 - 1300974. Most of the stained glass windows were made in the workshop of the O'Connors and there is work by Robert Bayne and Christopher Webb. The originally square font has been cut at some state to form an octagon, ruining some of the carving > 1301005 - 1301020. The rood screen > 1300931 is also largely original albeit restored and covered with dark varnish. There is a three figure brass > 1301039 on the west tower wall which dates from 1623 and features Agnes Brigge and her parents. This church is kept locked but a key is available on request. http://www.norfolkchurches.co.uk/ingoldisthorpe/ingoldisthorpe.htm

ImageDescription.value: The church of St Remigius in Roydon - Victorian floor tiles. The church of St Remigius > 1770044 has a round Norman tower with the top section and parapet added in Victorian times > 1770049. Nave and arcade date from the 13th century, the chancel was added a century later. The elaborately carved pulpit > 1770055 is Jacobean and has an hourglass stand attached to it. The church was extensively restored in the 19th century when the south aisle > 1770062 was added. The stained glass > 1770060 dates from that time. What now serves as a vestry on the south side of the chancel is the former medieval south porch.
